newsitem.title: ITALY: Judge - No crime for Italians to curse Virgin Mary.
newsitem.headline: Judge - No crime for Italians to curse Virgin Mary.

text.p: A judge has ruled that while it is still an offence in Italy to curse God it's no crime to blaspheme against the Virgin Mary, angering the Vatican and setting off a theological debate over the nature of divinity.

The decision freed young motorist Marco Catuzzi from a fine on Thursday when he was brought before a summary court in Avezzano, central Italy, for a litany of curses he poured forth three years ago when police stopped him for a traffic check.
Judge Francesco Centofanti acquitted Catuzzi over a torrent of expletives about Mary, the mother of God, and a variety of saints "because the fact is no longer seen as a crime".
What Catuzzi said about God did constitute a crime, Centofanti ruled, though he added that so much time had passed that punishment had lapsed under a statute of limitation.
Friday's L'Osservatore Romano, the semi-official Vatican newspaper, called the verdict offensive to the dignity of believers and to religion itself.

"Neither the Madonna nor the saints can be compared to God. No believer would go that far," Vatican theologian Gino Concetti wrote. "But freedom of religion demands...protection for the whole 'body' of the religion professed by the people."
Italy, where some of the crudest swear words have religious undertones, made blasphemy an offence in its penal code.

The Constitutional Court issued a little-noticed judgment about two months ago that the relevant article was valid only in so far as it applied to God but not to other figures venerated by Roman Catholics.
The offence carries a fine of 20,000 to 600,000 lire ($13 to $390).

Centofanti is believed to be the first judge to apply the ruling in a specific case, making certain of controversy in a country whose President Oscar Luigi Scalfaro, like Pope John Paul, is devoted to the Virgin Mary.
An Italian bishop, Armando Dini, said the ruling was "perfect from a theological standpoint because it affirms the uniqueness of God".
But he added: "It could be negative from a pastoral point of view though because it's certainly not nice to encourage people to blaspheme against the Madonna."
